Neonatal groundhogs emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 27 grams [Wwb = approximately 27 grams], a remarkably modest mass given the substantial body size these animals will eventually attain. This initial wet weight, recorded from captive litters within hours of parturition, places the newborn pup among the smallest relative to adult mass among North American sciurids. The transition from this altricial state to nutritional independence occurs after a prolonged period of maternal care, with weaning typically taking place at 46 days after birth [tx = 46 days after birth]; these values were obtained from individuals housed under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], reflecting the thermal regime of an actively nursing female. During the pre-weaning interval, the pup undergoes a dramatic transformation, gaining mass through the consumption of milk that is extraordinarily rich in lipids and proteins, a adaptation common among hibernating mammals whose young must accumulate sufficient reserves before their first winter. The entire gestation period, from successful copulation to live birth, spans 32 days [tg = 32 days] when the gravid female is maintained at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a short interval that is consistent with the rapid developmental schedules observed in other marmotine rodents.

By the time a young groundhog reaches the weaning stage, its body mass has increased substantially from the 27 grams recorded at birth, climbing to approximately 248 grams [Wwx = approximately 248 grams] at the cessation of lactation. This value represents the wet weight of a typical pup on the day it first consumes solid food independently, a milestone that signals the end of direct maternal provisioning. The timing of this transition, occurring 46 days after birth [tx = 46 days after birth] in animals maintained at a thermoneutral ambient temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is closely tied to the development of the digestive enzymes necessary for processing plant material. Field observations suggest that weaned juveniles immediately begin foraging on the tender shoots of grasses and forbs available near the natal burrow, though they may continue to share the maternal den for several additional weeks. The relatively high mass at weaning compared to the birth value reflects the rapid growth trajectory characteristic of a species that must achieve a critical body size before entering its first hibernation, a period of profound metabolic depression that can last for several months across the northern portions of its range.

As female groundhogs approach their first winter, they continue to grow and accumulate adipose stores, a process that is essential for surviving hibernation and for supporting the energetic demands of future reproduction. Sexual maturity in this species is not attained until well after the first season of hibernal dormancy; available data indicate that puberty occurs at 548 days since birth [tp = 548 days since birth] for females maintained under stable thermal conditions of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a finding derived from longitudinal studies of captive animals in which reproductive tract development was monitored via laparoscopy. This relatively late age at maturation is a common life-history strategy among medium-sized hibernating rodents that defer breeding until they have achieved a substantial fraction of their ultimate body size. The timing of this developmental milestone is presumably linked to the attainment of a critical fat reserve threshold, as females must be able to sustain both the metabolic costs of gestation and the subsequent lactation period without depleting the energy stores that are essential for their own survival.

The maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, recorded for this species in comprehensive trapping studies reaches 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams], a value that is typically observed in older, reproductively active males during the late summer period of hyperphagia that precedes hibernation. Females are generally smaller, though the largest individuals of both sexes converge on this upper size limit when conditions are favorable. Achieving this substantial mass requires several years of growth; the extreme longevity documented in the wild, with the oldest recorded individuals living up to 14 years [am = up to 14 years], provides ample time for somatic devel at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]opment. This lifespan estimate, confirmed through mark-recapture studies of a population in southern Ontario where core body temperature was consistently measured at 37 °C [T = 37 °C] during active periods, places the groundhog among the longest-lived members of the squirrel family, a pattern that correlates strongly with the species' investment in hibernation and its relatively slow pace of life. Over the course of that extended lifespan, a female can produce a substantial number of offspring.

Reproductive output in the groundhog is constrained by the species' seasonal breeding cycle and the brief window of opportunity following emergence from hibernation. Females typically produce a single litter each year, with the maximum litter size recorded in wild populations being 4.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4.5 pups per litter]; this fecundity is achieved only under optimal nutritional conditions, such as those found in agricultural landscapes with abundant forage. The maximum reproduction rate derived from this combination is approximately 4.5 pups per year [Ri = approximately 4.5 pups per year], a value consistent with a moderately K-selected life history. The combination of a modest litter size and a single annual reproductive bout results in a relatively low intrinsic rate of increase, a life-history pattern consistent with the species' role as a rodent that relies on individual survival and longevity rather than high fecundity to maintain population stability.
